A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EAMET study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and added material.

before.justification: v2 reports original model-editing experiments on CounterFact, ZsRE, and Wiki-recent, including robustness tests, ablations, and additional empirical results in Appendix F.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds computational-cost measurements, smaller-edit evaluations, embedding-similarity diagnostics, and additional hyperparameter results.

M1.justification: The embedding preparation, progressive residual alignment, KL-plus-MSE objective, and layer-update procedure are retained. Section 5 explains Equation (14) more explicitly, while Algorithm 1 and Appendix E remain unchanged. AlphaEdit-Aligned already appeared in v2.

E1.justification: CounterFact, ZsRE, Wiki-recent, the general-ability benchmarks, and the prefix and same-subject scenarios are retained. The new smaller-edit and diagnostic studies use existing datasets and tasks; varying edit counts does not introduce distinct task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain their baseline membership, including FT, MEND, ROME, MEMIT, PMET, and AlphaEdit in Table 4 and the existing AlphaEdit-Aligned comparison. New cost and edit-scale analyses reuse MEMIT without changing comparator membership in retained experiments.

E3.justification: New supplementary protocols evaluate 1–5,000 edits, profile runtime and GPU memory, measure key similarities over 1,000 sampled facts, and sweep M over 5, 10, 50, and 100. Existing benchmark settings and default hyperparameters are retained. The added statement that ROME runs sequentially with batch size one documents its setup without establishing a changed experiment.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds substantive analyses of which stages cause computational overhead, how performance varies with smaller edit counts, whether key geometry explains differences across models, and sensitivity to M. Existing loss and layer ablations, semantic analyses, and robustness tests remain. The editing-order study moves from v2 Appendix F.4 to v3 Section 6.3 rather than being newly added.

E5.justification: Both Table 4 captions report averages over five evaluations, and both versions disclose the same three editing-order shuffle seeds. v3 adds no confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars, or revised repeated-run practices.

E6.justification: Tables 11–15 add cost, edit-scale, key-similarity, and M-sensitivity results. For example, Table 13 reports CounterFact efficacy of 94.38% for EAMET versus 28.83% for MEMIT at 5,000 edits. Table 4 also changes ZsRE specificity values: EAMET rises from 38.87 to 39.87 on Deepseek-7B and from 40.39 to 42.39 on LLaMA3-8B, with accompanying baseline revisions changing rankings. Main efficacy and generalization entries remain unchanged. Fluency entries acquire an unexplained approximately 100-fold scale increase, which does not establish a performance gain.

T1.justification: The embedding-misalignment definition, Theorem 1, both corollaries, and the derivations and proofs in Appendices B–C are retained. The added efficacy label in Equation (15) and expanded objective explanation do not change the mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contribution: alignment addresses massive-editing failures and improves efficacy and robustness, with approximately 90% efficacy at 10,000 edits. Editing-order robustness was already claimed in v2's appendix; moving it into the main text does not introduce a new claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking twin-city failures to shared prompt prefixes, model differences to key separation, and large M to diluted alignment constraints. It also discusses practical overhead and asserts hyperparameter insensitivity. Some additions conflict with their evidence: Appendix F.8 describes Falcon's keys as more isolated despite Table 14's higher cosine similarities, and F.9 calls lambda_KL=2 the worst setting although Figure 10 peaks there.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents ROME's sequential batch-size-one execution, provides runtime and memory costs, and describes cosine computation through normalization and dot products. It changes the advertised code/data location from the project page to an anonymous artifact repository. Existing hardware, optimization settings, and default EAMET hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Chen et al. (2020), He et al. (2020), and Sun and Saenko (2016) around the alignment-loss discussion. Related-work wording also explicitly includes same-subject editing failures. The broader positioning relative to existing model-editing methods remains intact.

P1.justification: Changes include a localized rewrite explaining Equation (14), moving the editing-order discussion into Section 6.3, and extending the appendix organization. v3 also adds acknowledgments, separates ethics and reproducibility statements, and updates author annotations and publication headers. Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the appendix displays with Tables 11–15 covering cost breakdowns, edit-scale performance, model-wise key similarities, and M sensitivity. It moves the editing-order table into the main text and places Table 3 alongside its alignment discussion. Figure 1 and Table 3 receive explanatory caption additions. All ten existing figure graphics are retained without redrawing.

improvement.justification: v3 usefully supplies computational-cost evidence, smaller-edit results, M sensitivity, and clearer method documentation. However, newly added interpretations undermine confidence: Appendix F.8's separation argument conflicts with Table 14, while F.9 calls lambda_KL=2 the worst setting despite the retained Figure 10 and earlier explanation identifying it as best. Fluency values also change scale without a corresponding metric explanation. These benefits and reporting problems coexist, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall quality improvement.
